contents.title: Victory Speech - 2018 General Election
contents.content: Today, we stand at a historic crossroads. After 22 years of struggle, the people of Pakistan have voted for change. We promised them a Naya Pakistan, and now we have the opportunity to deliver. My government will focus on three key areas: First, we will build a welfare state modeled on the State of Madina, where every citizen has access to justice, education, and healthcare. Second, we will fight corruption at all levels. The plunder of national resources must end. We will strengthen institutions like the NAB and judiciary to ensure accountability. Third, we will revive the economy through job creation, exports, and reducing our dependence on loans. I want to thank the youth of Pakistan who believed in this vision. You are the future of this nation. To my opponents, I extend a hand of partnership. Pakistan's problems require all of us to work together. We will not seek revenge politics. The politics of victimization ends today. Our foreign policy will be based on partnership, not slavery. We want peaceful relations with all neighbors, especially India. The Kashmir issue must be resolved through dialogue. We will reset our relationship with the United States based on mutual respect and dignity. I promise you this: within 100 days, you will see visible changes. We will create 10 million jobs in 5 years, build 5 million houses for the poor, and plant 10 billion trees to combat climate change. This is not just a government; it's a movement for change. Pakistan Ka Matlab Kya? La Ilaha Illallah!
contents.summary: Imran Khan's victory speech after winning the 2018 general election, outlining his vision for a New Pakistan focused on welfare state, anti-corruption, and economic revival.
key_points: Economic revival through job creation and exports

contents.title: Speech at United Nations General Assembly on Kashmir
contents.content: I stand before you today representing not just Pakistan, but 1.3 billion Muslims who are watching what is happening in Kashmir. Eight million people have been under siege for 55 days. It is the longest curfew in the history of mankind. What is happening in Kashmir today is a test case for the United Nations. When 900,000 troops suppress 8 million people, what do you think is going to happen when the curfew is lifted? There will be a bloodbath. The ideology that India follows, the RSS ideology, inspired by the Nazi ideology, believes in racial and religious supremacy. This is the same ideology that led to the Holocaust. I asked myself: what is the world community doing while 8 million people are caged in the most militarized zone in the world? When the curfew is lifted, when they come out, there will be a reaction. The Pakistan army will not sit by and watch. We will fight till the last drop of our blood. But I want to make it clear: it will not be a war between two countries. It will be a war that will have consequences far beyond the borders of India and Pakistan. Both countries have nuclear weapons. And I want to ask the international community: should we witness nuclear war? Should we leave things as they are, hoping things will turn out alright? Or should the United Nations step in, as the Security Council promised in 1948, and hold a plebiscite in Kashmir? I am making this promise to the people of Kashmir today: As long as I am alive, I will be your ambassador. I will expose India's fascist ideology to the world. We want peace. We want to resolve this through dialogue. But India must lift the curfew, release the prisoners, and allow Kashmiris to decide their own future.
contents.summary: Imran Khan's powerful speech at the UN General Assembly highlighting the humanitarian crisis in Kashmir and calling for international intervention.
key_points: 55-day curfew in Kashmir described as longest in history
Warning of bloodbath when curfew is lifted
Comparison of RSS ideology to Nazi ideology
Nuclear war warning if situation escalates
Call for UN-supervised plebiscite in Kashmir
Promise to be Kashmir's ambassador to the world

contents.title: Interview with Al Jazeera on Afghanistan Policy
contents.event: Al Jazeera Talk to Al Jazeera
contents.content: Let me be very clear about Pakistan's position on Afghanistan. We want a peaceful, stable Afghanistan. For the last 40 years, Pakistan has suffered because of the instability in Afghanistan. We have hosted 4 million Afghan refugees. We have lost 80,000 lives in the war on terror. Our economy has suffered losses of over $150 billion. So we have paid a heavy price. Now, when people ask if Pakistan supports the Taliban, I say: which Pakistan are you talking about? The Pakistan under General Musharraf that supported the US invasion? Or Pakistan today that wants a political settlement? We have tried our best to bring the Taliban to the negotiating table. We cannot force them. We don't have that kind of control. What people don't understand is that the Taliban are not a homogeneous group. They have 60-70,000 armed fighters. No country can control them. The only solution is an inclusive government in Afghanistan where all factions are represented - Taliban, Tajiks, Hazaras, Uzbeks. A government that represents all of Afghanistan. Pakistan's role should be as a facilitator, not as someone who can dictate terms. The US spent $2 trillion, had 300,000 Afghan troops trained by NATO, had the most sophisticated weapons - if they couldn't control Afghanistan in 20 years, how can Pakistan control it? What we can do is use our influence to encourage the Taliban to form an inclusive government, respect human rights, especially women's rights, and not allow Afghan soil to be used for terrorism. That is in our interest because we don't want Pakist an to become a sanctuary for terrorists. We have already cleared our tribal areas at a great cost.
contents.summary: Interview discussing Pakistan's stance on Afghanistan, the Taliban, and regional stability following the US withdrawal.
key_points: 40 years of suffering from Afghan instability
Cannot control Taliban, only influence them
Emphasis on preventing terrorism from Afghan soil

contents.title: Tweet on Ehsaas Program Launch
contents.content: Today we launched Ehsaas - the biggest social safety net in Pakistan's history. This comprehensive poverty alleviation program will provide: 1) Financial assistance to 7 million families 2) Interest-free loans for small businesses 3) Undergraduate scholarships for students from low-income families 4) Nashonuma program for malnourished children 5) Langar for the homeless. Total budget: Rs. 260 billion. This is the Riyasat-e-Madina we promised - a state that takes care of its weakest citizens.
contents.summary: Announcement of Ehsaas program, Pakistan's largest social welfare initiative with Rs. 260 billion budget.

contents.title: Single National Curriculum Policy Document
contents.content: The Single National Curriculum (SNC) is a landmark reform in Pakistan's education system. For decades, we have had three parallel education systems: English-medium elite schools, Urdu-medium schools, and religious seminaries. This has created a class-divided society where opportunities depend on which school you can afford. The SNC aims to create a unified education system with the following features: 1) Common core curriculum for all schools (public, private, and madrassahs) from pre-primary to class 12. 2) Compulsory subjects include: Islamiyat, Pakistan Studies, English, Urdu, Mathematics, Science, and Social Studies. 3) Emphasis on critical thinking, creativity, and moral values. 4) Integration of religious education with modern subjects in madrassahs. 5) Standardized learning outcomes for all students regardless of school type. The curriculum has been developed with input from 400+ subject experts, educationists, and scholars. It aligns with international standards while preserving our Islamic and cultural values. Phase 1 (pre-primary to Class 5) was implemented in 2021. Phase 2 (Class 6-8) in 2022. Phase 3 (Class 9-12) will be implemented in 2023. This will take 10-15 years to show full results, but it is essential for creating an equal society. No child should be disadvantaged because of their family's economic status. The SNC ensures that whether you study in Aitchison College or a government school in a village, you receive the same quality education.
contents.summary: Overview of Single National Curriculum policy aimed at creating educational equality across Pakistan.
key_points: Unified curriculum for all schools (public, private, madrassahs)
Focus on critical thinking and moral values
citations: Government of Pakistan Official Policy Document

contents.title: Reflections on Cricket Career and Nation Building
contents.content: People ask me how my cricket career prepared me for politics. The answer is: everything I learned about leadership, I learned on the cricket field. When I became captain of Pakistan's cricket team in 1982, we were ranked 7th or 8th in the world. We had talent, but we lacked self-belief and discipline. My first job was to instill belief. I told the team: we can beat anyone in the world if we believe in ourselves and work as a unit. I created a culture of meritocracy. It didn't matter who your father was or which province you came from. If you performed, you played. If you didn't, you were dropped. I treated everyone equally - whether it was a star player or a newcomer. The 1992 World Cup victory was the culmination of this approach. We were written off after losing our first matches. Everyone said we should pack our bags and go home. But I told the team: we will fight like cornered tigers. We will give our 100% in every match. And if we lose, we lose with honor. That mindset changed everything. We won 5 consecutive matches and became world champions. What did I learn? 1) Never give up, no matter how difficult the situation. 2) Lead from the front. I bowled my heart out at age 39 with a damaged shoulder because my team needed me. 3) Build a team based on merit, not favoritism. 4) Create a vision and make everyone believe in it. These are the same principles I applied when building PTI. We started with just a few people in 1996. Everyone laughed at us. But we had a vision of a new Pakistan. And 22 years later, that vision became reality.
contents.summary: Imran Khan reflects on how his cricket career and 1992 World Cup victory shaped his leadership philosophy.
key_points: Leadership lessons from cricket applied to politics
Built Pakistan cricket team from 7th/8th to world champions
Never give up mentality - cornered tigers
Vision and belief as keys to success
